title: Episode 136: Franklin Pierce and the Caribbean Empire: The Gadsden Purchase and Ostend Manifesto
description:
While domestic politics descended into the nightmare of Bleeding Kansas, President Franklin Pierce pursued an audacious, aggressive foreign policy designed to project American power across the continent and the Caribbean. Influenced by the expansionist fervor of 'Young America,' Pierce believed that bold territorial acquisitions could unite a fractured nation under the banner of national greatness.

In eighteen fifty-three, Pierce dispatched railroad promoter James Gadsden to Mexico City to resolve border disputes and acquire land for a southern transcontinental railroad. For ten million dollars, the United States acquired nearly thirty thousand square miles of rugged desert in modern-day southern Arizona and New Mexico—the Gadsden Purchase—finalizing the contiguous continental borders of the United States that endure to this day.

Far more explosive was Pierce's secret campaign to acquire the Spanish island colony of Cuba. Southern planters viewed the sugar-rich island as the ultimate prize: a territory that could yield two or three new slave states to balance Northern power. In eighteen fifty-four, Pierce's ministers to Great Britain, France, and Spain—including future President James Buchanan—met secretly in Ostend, Belgium, to draft a confidential dispatch. Known as the 'Ostend Manifesto,' the diplomats declared that the United States should offer Spain one hundred and twenty million dollars for Cuba, and if Spain refused, America would be fully justified 'by every law, human and divine, in wresting it from Spain' by military force. When the secret manifesto leaked to the press, Northern outrage detonated, exposing a brazen imperial conspiracy. Here is George with the full story.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we conclude our exploration of President Franklin Pierce with his ambitious, controversial quest for territorial expansion. In the eighteen-fifties, American visionaries dreamed not only of spanning the continent from coast to coast, but of establishing a sprawling tropical empire in the Caribbean. From buying desert valleys for transcontinental rails to plotting the military seizure of Spanish Cuba, Pierce's foreign policy pushed America to the brink of international war. Here is George with the full story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE DREAM OF 'YOUNG AMERICA'
When Franklin Pierce entered the White House in eighteen fifty-three, he was captured by the romantic, aggressive spirit of 'Young America.' Spearheaded by expansionist Democrats, Young America was a geopolitical philosophy that believed the United States was destined to bring republican democracy and commercial dominion to the entire Western Hemisphere. Pierce declared in his inaugural address that his administration would not be deterred by 'any timid forebodings of evil from expansion.'
Nowhere was this expansionist hunger more ravenous than in the American South. Following the admission of California as a free state in eighteen fifty, Southern slaveholders felt encircled. The Western frontier north of Texas offered little fertile ground for plantation cotton. Southern visionaries began casting predatory eyes southward toward the Caribbean basin and Central America—a tropical expanse they envisioned as a vast 'Golden Circle' of new slave states that would dominate the global production of sugar, coffee, and cotton.
Private American adventurers, known as 'filibusters'—from the Spanish word for freebooters—launched unauthorized private military invasions of Latin American lands. Men like William Walker, the 'grey-eyed man of destiny,' invaded Baja California and later seized control of Nicaragua, declaring himself president and legalizing slavery with the covert sympathy of Southern politicians. But for the Pierce administration, the supreme prize of the Caribbean lay just ninety miles off the coast of Florida: the Spanish island jewel of Cuba.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: JAMES GADSDEN AND THE IRON TRAIL
Before turning to Cuba, Pierce addressed an urgent, practical domestic challenge: connecting the newly acquired wealth of California to the rest of the nation. In the early eighteen-fifties, thousands of gold miners and merchants were forced to travel to California either by perilous six-month wagon journeys across the Plains, or by dangerous sea voyages around Cape Horn or through the malaria-infested jungles of Panama. The nation desperately needed a transcontinental railroad.
Secretary of War Jefferson Davis of Mississippi was determined that the first transcontinental line should run through the South. Davis commissioned federal army surveys that proved the best geographic route—avoiding the towering snow-covered Sierra Nevada and Rocky Mountain passes—lay south of the Gila River. But there was a critical obstacle: the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo had drawn the Mexican border just north of the Mesilla Valley, leaving the vital low-altitude mountain passes inside Mexican territory.
In eighteen fifty-three, Pierce appointed James Gadsden, a prominent South Carolina railroad executive and former soldier, as minister to Mexico. Gadsden was instructed to negotiate a boundary treaty with Mexican dictator General Antonio López de Santa Anna. Mexico was bankrupt, and Santa Anna desperately needed cash to pay his army and suppress internal rebellions. Gadsden initially sought to purchase all of Baja California and northern Sonora, but Mexican national pride resisted. After intense, dramatic negotiations in Mexico City, Gadsden and Santa Anna signed the Gadsden Treaty on December thirtieth, eighteen fifty-three.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: COMPLETING THE CONTIGUOUS MAP
Under the treaty, the United States agreed to pay Mexico ten million dollars—an enormous sum at the time—in exchange for twenty-nine thousand six hundred and seventy square miles of territory in modern-day southern Arizona and southwestern New Mexico. The acquisition included the fertile Mesilla Valley, the strategic town of Tucson, and the gentle mountain passes south of the Gila River essential for railroad construction.
When the treaty reached the Senate, Northern anti-slavery senators, suspicious that Jefferson Davis was using federal funds to build a Southern railroad to expand slave territory, trimmed the purchase area and reduced the price. But the treaty passed, and President Pierce signed it into law in June eighteen fifty-four.
The Gadsden Purchase was an enduring geographic milestone. It settled the final bitter border disputes remaining from the Mexican-American War and established the permanent contiguous southern boundary of the United States. Today, the Southern Pacific Railroad and Interstate Ten run directly through the mountain passes purchased by James Gadsden. It was the final piece of the continental jigsaw puzzle, completing the forty-eight contiguous United States. But as Pierce celebrated this triumph in the desert, his Caribbean ambitions were detonating an international crisis.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE PEARL OF THE ANTILLES
For decades, American statesmen had coveted Cuba, the 'Pearl of the Antilles.' Rich in sugarcane, tobacco, and coffee, and garrisoned by Spanish imperial troops, Cuba held the strategic keys to the Gulf of Mexico and the mouth of the Mississippi River. Thomas Jefferson had written that Cuba's addition to the American union would complete the empire of liberty, and John Quincy Adams had famously described Cuba as an 'apple' that would naturally fall into America's lap by the laws of political gravitation.
In the eighteen-fifties, the question became an emergency for Southern planters. Spain was coming under intense diplomatic pressure from Great Britain to abolish slavery in Cuba. Southern slaveholders were haunted by the terrifying prospect of 'Africanization'—that Spain would free Cuba's four hundred thousand enslaved Black laborers, creating an armed Black republic just ninety miles from Florida, which they feared would incite slave uprisings across the American South.
President Pierce was determined to acquire the island. He appointed Pierre Soulé of Louisiana, a flamboyant, hot-headed French-born political exile, as American minister to Spain. Soulé was an aggressive expansionist who favored armed intervention. Arriving in Madrid, Soulé challenged the French ambassador to a sword duel over a minor insult to his wife's dress, shot the ambassador in the leg, and openly plotted with Spanish anti-monarchical revolutionaries, making himself thoroughly despised by the Spanish royal court.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BLACK WARRIOR AFFAIR
In February eighteen fifty-four, the simmering tensions exploded into open confrontation. The American merchant steamship Black Warrior, on a regular run between New York and Mobile, Alabama, docked in Havana harbor. Spanish customs authorities, enforcing strict maritime regulations, discovered a technical error in the ship's cargo manifest: the clerk had marked the cargo as 'in ballast' rather than listing nine hundred bales of cotton.
Spanish authorities seized the Black Warrior, hauled down the American flag, confiscated the cargo, and placed the American captain under arrest, imposing a massive fine. In Washington, Southern expansionists smelled blood in the water. Hot-headed congressmen shouted that the honor of the American flag had been desecrated, demanding an immediate declaration of war against Spain and the naval invasion of Cuba.
In Madrid, Pierre Soulé seized the incident. Without waiting for instructions from the State Department, Soulé issued an arrogant, forty-eight-hour ultimatum to the Spanish government, demanding an indemnity of three hundred thousand dollars and the dismissal of all Spanish officials in Cuba. The Spanish foreign minister completely ignored Soulé's ultimatum and resolved the Black Warrior dispute directly with the ship's owners in Havana. Soulé was humiliated, but Secretary of State William L. Marcy saw an opportunity to mount a coordinated diplomatic offensive.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE SECRET SUMMIT AT OSTEND
In August eighteen fifty-four, Secretary of State Marcy instructed America's three premier diplomats in Europe to meet in private: Pierre Soulé in Spain, John Y. Mason in France, and James Buchanan, the prestigious minister to Great Britain. Their mission was to formulate a unified, confidential strategy to acquire Cuba.
In October eighteen fifty-four, the three diplomats met secretly in the quiet Belgian resort town of Ostend, before moving to Aix-la-Chapelle in Prussia to finalize their report. Soulé dominated the discussions, while James Buchanan, eying the eighteen fifty-six Democratic presidential nomination and eager for Southern support, lent his legal and diplomatic polish to the document. On October eighteenth, eighteen fifty-four, they signed their confidential dispatch to Washington: the 'Ostend Manifesto.'
The manifesto was a breathtaking document of imperial arrogance. The diplomats argued that Cuba was geographically and economically essential to the United States. They recommended that the United States offer Spain up to one hundred and twenty million dollars to purchase the island. But then came the explosive, fatal paragraph.
The diplomats wrote: 'Does Cuba, in the possession of Spain, seriously endanger our internal peace and the existence of our cherished Union? Should this question be answered in the affirmative, then, by every law, human and divine, we shall be justified in wresting it from Spain, if we have the power! Under such circumstances we ought neither to count the cost nor regard the odds which Spain might enlist against us.' It was an explicit declaration of intent to wage an aggressive, unprovoked war of conquest.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE LEAK AND THE DEATH OF THE CARIBBEAN DREAM
Secretary of State Marcy was horrified when he opened the Ostend dispatch in Washington. The timing could not have been more disastrous. The Pierce administration was already reeling from the catastrophic backlash over the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and congressional mid-term elections were only weeks away. Marcy ordered the document kept in strictest secrecy.
Inevitably, the secret leaked. In early eighteen fifty-five, the contents of the Ostend Manifesto were published in the New York Herald. The reaction across the North and throughout European capitals was one of unbridled outrage and disgust. Northern newspapers bitterly denounced the manifesto as the 'Manifesto of the Brigands'—a shameless, criminal attempt by Southern slaveholders to drag the nation into a bloody foreign war to expand human bondage.
European powers condemned the United States as an aggressive, lawless bully. In Congress, Free-Soil and Republican representatives mounted blistering attacks against Pierce. Panicked by the political backlash, Secretary of State Marcy publicly disavowed the manifesto, formally repudiating Pierre Soulé's actions. Humiliated and abandoned, Soulé resigned his post in fury.
The leaked Ostend Manifesto permanently killed any hope of acquiring Cuba. It exposed the deep, irreconcilable fracture at the heart of American expansionism: that every square mile of new territory was no longer seen as a blessing of liberty, but as a lethal weapon in the battle over slavery.
Franklin Pierce had completed the contiguous map of the American Southwest with the Gadsden Purchase, but his dream of a tropical Caribbean empire collapsed in disgrace—leaving the nation to turn its gaze inward toward the inescapable, gathering storm of civil war.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Franklin Pierce's expansionist foreign policy completed the continental boundaries of the United States with the Gadsden Purchase, but his secret bid for Cuba shattered against the growing moral opposition to slavery. Next week, we turn to America's fifteenth President, James Buchanan—the bachelor statesman from Pennsylvania whose meddling in the Supreme Court's Dred Scott decision and paralysis during the winter of secession plunged the nation into the abyss of civil war. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
